attempts.summary: Built a redundant dual-link fabric between node1 (SONiC) and node2 (SONiC), each serving its own private host — node3 behind node1, node4 behind node2. The two direct links (eth1+eth2) were bonded into a Linux kernel bond0 in balance-rr mode (LACP/802.3ad was tried first but never converged since these are direct point-to-point virtio links with no switch to relay LACPDUs; balance-rr requires no protocol negotiation, uses carrier-based miimon, and round-robins every packet across both links). node1 routes 192.168.10.0/24 (node3's LAN) via bond0 to node2, and node2 routes 192.168.20.0/24 (node4's LAN) via bond0 to node1. Verified genuine dual-link load spreading via per-interface tx counters, then disrupted one link (eth1 admin-down) while a continuous ping ran between node3 and node4: zero packet loss throughout, traffic shifted fully to eth2, and traffic resumed on eth1 immediately after restoring it. Config was persisted via a systemd oneshot unit (redundant-uplink.service, enabled) running /usr/local/sbin/setup-bond.sh on node1/node2, and via ifupdown drop-ins on node3/node4 (Ubuntu 16.04). All four nodes were then restarted one at a time (SONiC nodes via systemctl reboot, Ubuntu nodes via sudo reboot), each polled back to reachability, each showing a changed /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id, and each showing full recovery: bond0 both slaves MII up, correct IPs/routes restored automatically, and node3<->node4 end-to-end ping succeeding with 0% loss after every restart. Final post-all-reboot check reconfirmed both bond links actively carrying traffic in balance.
